questions.q: Why does this course follow one app, Bazaar, from start to end?
options: Because one app is less work to write
So every tool comes from a real problem, and you always know why you learn it
Because Bazaar is a famous real company
So you never need to write any code
questions.explain: As Bazaar grows, real problems appear. Each problem brings the next tool, so you learn the why and the trade-offs, not just the how.

questions.q: In the lab, 100 customers arrive at once. Why does the slowest one wait over 2 seconds?
options: The internet is slow
Python is a slow language
The backend has one worker, so requests wait in a queue one after another
The products file is too big
questions.explain: One worker handles one request at a time. 100 requests × about 23 ms each ≈ 2.3 seconds for the last one in the line.

options: A bug that crashes the server
The narrowest point in a system, which slows everything down
A kind of database
A type of Python error
questions.explain: Like the neck of a bottle, it limits how fast everything can flow. Always find it before choosing a fix.

questions.q: In which level does Bazaar face the Diwali sale and add load balancing and sharding?
options: Level 1: Foundations
Level 3: Data
Level 5: Scaling
Level 2: Core backend
questions.explain: Level 5 is about scaling. One server and one database are not enough, so Bazaar spreads the work across many machines.

questions.q: A lab shows an error. What should you do first?
options: Delete the lab and start again
Read the error message from the bottom, then the lab's Stuck? section and the logs
Copy the reference solution right away
Restart your computer
questions.explain: The last line of an error usually says exactly what went wrong. Most problems are solved before you ever need the solution.

questions.q: (Going deeper) One worker needs about 23 ms per request. What is its throughput, at most?
options: About 23 requests per second
About 43 requests per second
About 1,000 requests per second
It has no limit
questions.explain: 1000 ms ÷ 23 ms ≈ 43. In the lab, 300 requests took about 7.2 seconds: about 42 per second.

questions.q: (Going deeper) What is the difference between latency and throughput?
options: They are the same
Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests finish per second
Latency is for databases; throughput is for networks
Throughput is how long one request takes
questions.explain: When more requests arrive than the throughput allows, a queue builds up and the latency grows.

questions.q: (Going deeper) Threads cut the wait from 2,300 ms to 60 ms when the work was a 20 ms sleep. When the work was 20 ms of CPU work, threads helped much less. Why?
options: Sleep is faster than CPU work
Waiting threads don't block each other, but Python threads take turns for CPU work
The CPU was broken
Threads only work on Mac
questions.explain: While one thread waits, others can run. But only one thread at a time runs Python code (the GIL), so CPU work doesn't spread over threads.
